instructions: Read the original passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
A fictional neighborhood group wants to run an art workshop. Their aim is to give adults a chance to try a small creative task together. The organizer, Priya, writes a proposal and asks the group to compare two ways of displaying the work. The event is planned for Thursday at two, but the group will check the room booking before sending the final notice.

The first option is to place artwork on a long table. Its advantage is that visitors can sit nearby and discuss each piece. A disadvantage is that the table leaves less space for people to move. The alternative is a display on two boards beside the wall. One concern is whether the boards will be stable enough, so Priya will ask the building manager for guidance before the event.

The designer makes a small prototype from paper. She uses a pencil to draw a simple frame and a little glue to attach a sample label. The prototype is only a model for discussion, not a finished display. The group notices a problem: the label on the first version is too small to read from the doorway. Their solution is to try a larger label and check it from the same place again.

Another issue is the budget. In the invented example, the table display costs twenty-six dollars in materials and the board display costs twenty-two. Those numbers do not include the room or staff time. The group chooses the board approach for the trial, provided the manager confirms that it can be used. A suggestion from one member is to keep the table method available if the boards cannot be arranged.

The group plans to divide the work into short tasks. Priya will assign one person to prepare the cards and another to check the calendar. A volunteer is meeting the room manager on Tuesday to confirm the booking. Each contribution matters: one person can welcome guests, while another can lead the demonstration. No one needs to finish a professional artwork during the session.

The leaflet will explain what visitors can try. A longer brochure will describe the two display choices and their costs. The group also wants to include photography, but will ask each participant before sharing a recognizable image. That is the group's own plan, not a claim about rules everywhere. Priya hopes the workshop will encourage creativity without forcing everyone to use the same style.

Before leaving, the members read the proposal once more. They agree to check the room, materials and wording on the cards. The designer will bring the revised model, and Priya will send the final invitation only after the booking is confirmed. A small plan is easier to discuss when its choices and uncertainties are visible.
